The Saulteaux is a small community located on the banks of the St. Lawrence River in eastern Ontario, Canada.
In 1892, A. J. Meyers became the first man to fish for silver in the area and in 1895 he purchased a pond that had been used by the Indians as a shelter during an Indian raid. The lake was named after him. Today it serves as one of the most popular fishing spots in northern Ontario with hundreds of anglers coming to enjoy this unique spot.
The history of the Saulteaux dates back to the 1600s when Europeans came across Lake Superior and set up fur trading posts along its shores. Later they brought their own settlers who established settlements around the lakeshore where the water was good enough for hunting and fishing. In 1743, Sir John Colborne established a settlement at the mouth of the Saint Lawrence River which would become known as Fort Saulteau. This fort was destroyed in 1746 due to Iroquois attacks but the river continues to be a source of food for wildlife and people today.

The East Bay Battlefield is a historic site and a city park in San Francisco, California. It was originally owned by the West Enders, but after their defeat in World War II it became part of the city’s police force.
In 1952, under pressure from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the Board of Supervisors decided to divide up the land into two separate districts: one for private use and another for public use. This division was based on the assumption that the 80-acre parcel had been acquired by the City of San Francisco when they were involved with the World War II aerial bombardment. The land would later be designated as the San Francisco Municipal Airport (SFMO).
Over the years, both portions have been used for commercial and industrial purposes. Today the area known as “the Shriver Line” is dominated by many high rises, towers, and skyscrapers. Other notable structures include the Olympic Dome, the 36th Street Station building, the Old Sacramento Building, and the Pacifica Hotel. The former home of Sutter’s Ferry, the current headquarters of the Department of Transportation, is now a popular stop along Route 42 and Santa Barbara Boulevard.

What is a cultural legacy?
A legacy is an asset that has been passed down from one generation to the next. These assets are intangible and include things like, for example:
- The skills or knowledge of a particular group
- An event, product or service
- A piece of artwork or photograph
- A set of techniques used in the production process
- A heritage item that was manufactured
An inheritance can be anything but tangible. It includes items such as a collection of artworks, photographs or historic objects. It also includes those that have been passed down through generations; something that is valuable to us today. For instance, if you were lucky enough to own a piece of art, it would be passed on by tradition to your children.
How do I create my own cultural legacy?
The following list describes some of the ways you can make a new cultural legacy. There are many other ways you can use this information to get started.
Tips for creating your own cultural legacy
1. Share your story with others – share your personal stories so they know how special these resources really are!
2. Seek out local businesses who might be able to provide you with relevant materials. Find out what their customers think about the material you’re using.

The temperature at which a liquid boils is called its boiling point. If you were to drop an ice cube in your mouth, the ice would boil (turn into steam). This vapor can be formed by both evaporation and condensation (the process where water molecules are forced to collide with other atoms). But water has no such ideal boiling point—it boils at a lower temperature than any other substance. So how does it get there? Well, since water exists as a liquid, this means that when water evaporates, it cools off, making it less dense. In turn, vaporization makes it denser again until it reaches its final state, which is its boiling point. That's why we have hot or cold water; it never boils unless something goes wrong.

Climate change is already having an impact on the oceans and coral reefs. The research she has conducted over the past few years reveals that warming temperatures are disrupting their delicate balance as well as destroying corals. Scientists estimate that 90% of all ocean fish could be extinct by mid century if global greenhouse gas emissions continue unabated.
